problem: The claim that the nine-qubit (Shor) code has transversal Hadamard and phase gates is false. Its stabilizer is not preserved by H on all nine qubits: H maps the code to a different code (X and Z generators swap), so H^⊗9 is not a logical gate for it. The same failure applies to the phase gate S. Only the transversal CNOT holds for that code, so a student would learn a wrong example of transversal Clifford gates.
fix: For the seven-qubit Steane code, transversal CNOT, Hadamard and phase gates are all available. The nine-qubit Shor code gives a transversal CNOT but not a transversal Hadamard. Together these gates generate the Clifford group.

problem: The threshold range quoted for concatenated codes, 10⁻² to 10⁻³, is too optimistic and contradicts the chapter's own Beyond note that surface codes tolerate higher error rates than concatenated codes. Standard estimates put concatenated-code thresholds at roughly 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁴ under realistic noise, with optimistic ideal-circuit estimates near 10⁻³; surface codes are the ones near 10⁻².
fix: Typical threshold estimates are around 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁴ for concatenated codes under realistic noise models, with optimistic ideal-circuit estimates near 10⁻³. Surface codes reach about 10⁻², which is why hardware groups favour them. Detailed threshold calculations are beyond this unit.

where: Section 3, first sentence of syndrome extraction
problem: Saying the ancilla is prepared in |0> covers only Z-type stabilizers. For X-type stabilizers the ancilla must be prepared in |+> (Hadamard on |0>), and the coupling is by CNOTs in the other direction. A student meeting a circuit diagram with |+> ancillas will be confused.
fix: A syndrome extraction circuit couples data qubits to an ancilla prepared in |0> for Z-type stabilizers and in |+> for X-type stabilizers. The ancilla is measured; the data are not measured.

problem: The sentence 'The ancilla touches only the syndrome step, not the data path' is misleading: during syndrome extraction the ancilla is coupled to the data qubits by CNOTs, which is exactly how the syndrome is read. What is true is that the ancilla is not a data qubit and carries no logical information.
fix: The ancilla is used only in the syndrome-extraction step: it is coupled to the data qubits there, then measured. It carries no logical information and is never part of the logical output.

problem: The definition covers only two-block gates. Transversal Hadamard and phase gates act inside one block, applying the physical gate to every qubit of that block. Also 'two code blocks' should allow one or two.
fix: A transversal gate acts on one or two code blocks: it applies the same physical gate to every qubit of a block (single-qubit gate) or between corresponding qubits of two blocks (two-qubit gate), touching each physical qubit at most once.

where: Quiz Q5, answer (and Section 3 wording 'fresh or verified')
problem: 'A fresh or verified ancilla prevents its own error from entering the data' is too strong. Verification and freshness make an ancilla fault unlikely; they do not rule it out, and an undetected ancilla error can still propagate into the data.
fix: It interacts with the data qubits and is then measured, giving syndrome information without measuring the data. Using a fresh or verified ancilla makes it unlikely that an ancilla fault passes into the data, but does not make it impossible.

problem: 'These gates form the Clifford group' is loose: the set of gates that can be done transversally for one code is a subgroup of the Clifford group, usually a small finite set, not the whole group.
fix: The transversal gates of a code form a subgroup of the Clifford group; for the Steane code this subgroup includes CNOT, Hadamard and phase.
